_doc: Hand-maintained source of fish.json (built by tools/build_fish.py; see its header). Edit this file, then re-run the build.
sources: where circle 3 comes from (teaching nodes cite them in srcs). leftOut: families decided out of circle 3, with why. retired: ids taken out; never reuse them.

keys: the regional identification keys (Pierre, 2026-11-04). In its region a key is the reference for fish groups: every teaching node in the game attaches to one of its groups (rule S3); a region with no key has no such rule, and a key for another region is data only (no code change).
id: stable. region: {name, area: what the key covers}. cite: the full citation (the families page credit line); short: the short form used everywhere else (one edit changes both).

src: what it was transcribed from. groups: the key's groups in its order: n, title (exact), pages [first, last], labels: [label as the key prints it, [WoRMS accepted names it covers], note when the mapping needs one].
The build gives a node the group of the first label met walking up WoRMS from each of its ref (a subfamily label wins over its family's: Parrotfishes over Wrasses).

look: look-alike groups of the book's families declared beyond the IMR course, each {src, key (the key whose family labels the ids name: applied only while it is in force), groups [[family ids]], note {"a|b": words}}: every pair of a group is a look-alike both ways, its source in the families' lsrc (tools/build_fish.py add_families). Pierre, 2026-11-06, from experience; they seed the traps and the confusion groups until pooled fish answers exist.
deploy: this deployment: its region and the key in force there (keys id). Another deployment changes this and its own keys.
teach: the teaching tree, in game order: the 27 IMR entries (circle 1) in the order of the IMR fish presentation, then circle 2, then circle 3.
id: stable id, never the name; never reuse or renumber. name: as IMR names it. fam: the family as IMR writes it.
circle: 1 IMR core, 2 seen sometimes on SVS video, 3 opt-in beyond IMR.

keyGroup: {key id: group n} an explicit choice, only where the node's references span two groups of that key, or {key id: null} with keyWhy while a node in the game waits for a decision (the build lists it); the build fails otherwise.
Circle 3 is not PDF-based (Pierre, 2026-11-03): the fish families divers want to recognise, muck diving above all (why, srcs),
with their species confirmed near Dauin (build_fish.py near_dauin: Pierre's own, Research Grade by 2+ observers within 40 km, or the IMR PDF list), plus winks.
src: imr (the presentation), pdf (a family of the EventMeasure reference PDF), diver (circle 3), wink.

wink (Pierre): an unmistakable species, fun to meet, a light bonus rather than ID training (note says why), shown as a rare surprise card: choices = [teach id, tongue-in-cheek label] absurd distractors from our own entries, right / wrong = feedback lines.
sign: false when the entry is taught but not on the presentation's dive-sign list.
ref: WoRMS names (or AphiaIDs) of the reference nodes it covers; not: reference nodes inside them that it leaves out.
A species belongs to the teaching node whose ref holds its nearest ancestor (most specific wins, not excludes),
its genus being the genus of its written name (Chromis agilis stays under Chromis; WoRMS has it in Pycnochromis).
pdf: the PDF section headings (family token) whose species it should hold (cross-check printed by the build).
sl: presentation slides. cues, look ([teach id, how to tell it apart]), phase: short English from the presentation.
sub: named sub-entries taught inside an entry (same fields; their species are a subset of the entry's).

juv: the juveniles of a circle-1 entry (research note of 2026-11-04, classes and rules approved by Pierre; src: the sources, by: Pierre when he gave it too). cls A: distinctive and recognisable, they help learn the family early; B: nondescript, confusing or resembling another family, taught later; C: broadly like the adults; ns: no juvenile-specific source found (ask an IMR trainer); mixed: per genus or species, early = the genera or species whose juveniles show early, late = those resembling another family or alike across species. trait: what to teach about them (sourced); obs: what Pierre observed (his own words, 2026-11-04). Mimicry is always a hypothesis: written as resembles or has been suggested. A juvenile photo is judged on the other criteria only (no juvenile cap) when its entry is A or its species is in early; every other juvenile keeps the cap: B and late for good (explanation cards later), C, ns and the rest provisionally (judging/FISH.md).

dimorph: true when the presentation's phase lines say the sexes or colour phases look different (Parrotfish, Anthias): every photo shows one of those forms, so none is among the very easy photos of its first questions (judging/FISH.md).

start: the starter core, the circle-1 entries a new player meets first, before any other opens (model.js openPick, a record's first). Pierre's fish-ID design (2026-11-04): four easy, readable families first, Butterflyfishes, Angelfishes, Damselfishes & Anemonefishes, Surgeonfishes & Tangs.
species: one per line: PDF order, the slides, winks, then Dauin species of circle 3. id: stable, never reuse.
name: as written in the PDF, i.e. as EventMeasure names it (its fixed pick list may lag WoRMS): it stays the name shown and
expected; the build adds the WoRMS accepted name beside it (now). A PDF species of a family in no circle, or not
confirmed in the Philippines, stays in fish.json out of the game (the future Fish ID Key holds every PDF species).
Confirmed = Research Grade on iNaturalist, or one of Pierre's own (ppericard) observations identified to the species,
even Needs ID (he names a species only when very sure); his only. The build computes it (presence()).
as: the name to look up when the written one does not resolve (hand fix of a typo or wrapped name).
common: common name as in the PDF (never corrected). src: pdf (default), slides, dauin, wink.
sec: PDF section (family token of its heading). pdf: PDF pages. cs: rank on the PDF cheatsheet (24 most sighted).
sl: slide where the presentation names it. check: a point for Pierre to check against EventMeasure (e.g. a likely slip).

sources.pierre: Pierre's list of families divers want to recognise, 2026-11-03
sources.dtw: Dive The World, Dumaguete & Dauin dive sites: https://www.dive-the-world.com/diving-sites-philippines-dumaguete-dauin.php
sources.mcp: Marine Conservation Philippines, Muck diving in Dauin: https://marineconservationphilippines.org/muck-diving-dauin-marine-life/
sources.uwpg: Underwater Photography Guide, Muck-diving and macro-diving critters: https://uwphotographyguide.com/node/102
sources.inat: iNaturalist, Research Grade observations within 40 km of Dauin (species kept: at least 2)

leftOut.Gobiidae: Gobies: not in circle 3 (Pierre, 2026-11-03): tiny, hard to find on dives, of little interest to most divers. The PDF gobies stay in fish.json out of the game, for the Fish ID Key.
leftOut.Gobiesocidae: Clingfishes: taken out of circle 3 (Pierre, 2026-11-04): not among the family labels of the identification key in force (rule S3). No PDF species; their two Dauin species were retired with them.

keys.cite: Allen, G., Steene, R., Humann, P. & DeLoach, N. (2015). Reef Fish Identification – Tropical Pacific, 2nd ed. New World Publications. ISBN 978-1-878348-60-9
keys.src: the book's index of its Twenty Identification Groups (group title, pages, the family labels under its drawings), transcribed 2026-11-04 from Pierre's screenshots (Drive, 01_ReefRecall/01_Ressources/Fish ID Groups - Indo Pacific)

groups.title: Small Ovals – Damselfishes
labels: anemonefishes (WoRMS files Amphiprion directly under Pomacentridae, so Pomacentridae carries them)

groups.title: Silvery
labels: grunters as Terapontidae; to check whether the book also means the javelin grunters (Pomadasys, Haemulidae)
WoRMS splits the halfbeaks into two families

groups.title: Slender Schoolers/Colorful
labels: WoRMS ranks the anthias as a family (Anthiadidae), formerly the subfamily Anthiadinae of Serranidae

groups.title: Heavy Bodies/Large Lips
labels: WoRMS files the soapfishes in Grammistidae and, for Diploprion, in Liopropomatidae (Diploprioninae)

groups.title: Swim with Pectoral Fins – Parrotfishes
labels: WoRMS: the subfamily Scarinae of Labridae

groups.title: Cryptic Crevice Dwellers
labels: the Indo-Pacific basslets as Liopropoma (Liopropomatidae); to check against the book's pages

groups.title: Small, Elongate Bottom Dwellers – Gobies
labels: WoRMS splits the gobies into Gobiidae and Oxudercidae

groups.title: Odd-Shaped Bottom Dwellers
labels: the seabed batfishes (Ogcocephalidae), not the Platax batfishes (Ephippidae, group 1)
the lefteye flounders; to check whether the book includes other flounder families

teach.name: Damselfish
cues: Tail from deeply forked to rounded
Most common family in IMR surveys

sub.name: Chromis
cues: Plankton feeders in large schools above the coral

juv.note: Dascyllus juveniles: black with white blotches, still clearly Dascyllus. Chromis and Pomacentrus: no juvenile source found.

teach.name: Butterflyfish
cues: Small terminal mouth: feeds on coral polyps
Dorsal, tail and anal fins curve into a disc
look: Angelfish: spine on the gill cover, iridescent blue

sub.name: Bannerfish
cues: No yellow on the saddle (Moorish idol has one)

juv.note: Same disc shape; some Chaetodon juveniles add a rear dorsal black spot.

teach.name: Angelfish
cues: Oval like a butterflyfish, continuous dorsal fin
Spine on the gill cover (opercular spine)
look: Butterflyfish: no opercular spine, no iridescent blue
phase: Juveniles look very different from adults

juv.note: Pomacanthus juveniles: striking patterns unlike the adults (e.g. dark blue with electric blue and white rings). Centropyge: no juvenile source found.

teach.name: Spadefish
cues: Black band over the eye in adults
phase: Juvenile and adult colours can differ completely
The juvenile pinnate spadefish mimics a toxic flatworm

juv.trait: very tall fins: greatly elongated dorsal and anal fins
juv.obs: They look much bigger than they are: very elongated dorsal and anal fins on a tiny body; as they grow, the body grows while the overall height hardly changes (Pierre, 2026-11-04)
juv.note: A resemblance to floating leaves or flatworms has been suggested, not established.

teach.name: Moorish Idol
cues: Only one species in the family
Yellow on the body and a yellow saddle
look: Bannerfish: no yellow on the saddle

juv.note: No source compares juvenile and adult colour; the horns are an adult feature.

teach.name: Surgeonfish & Unicornfish
cues: Scalpel on the tail base (caudal peduncle)
Moderate fishing vulnerability in the Philippines

sub.name: Surgeonfish
cues: One scalpel on the tail base

sub.name: Unicornfish
cues: Two scalpels on the tail base

juv.note: Acanthurus pyroferus juveniles resemble Centropyge pygmy angelfish (another family). Naso, Zebrasoma, Ctenochaetus: no juvenile issue retained or no source.

teach.name: Rabbitfish
cues: Slightly elongated mouth with puckered lips

juv.note: Juveniles look similar to the adults (Siganus puellus); same body plan.

teach.name: Parrotfish
cues: Swims with the pectoral fins, flapping like a bird
look: Wrasse: thick lips, no visible teeth
phase: Males colourful, females dark or dull
Intermediate and terminal phases look different

juv.note: Small juveniles are striped, alike across species, and change pattern as they grow.

teach.name: Wrasse
cues: Swims with the pectoral fins, flapping like a bird
Huge variety of sizes, shapes and colours

juv.note: Coris gaimard juveniles: red to orange with black-edged white saddles; Novaculichthys juveniles are unmistakable (a resemblance to drifting seaweed has been suggested). Most Halichoeres and Thalassoma juveniles look alike across species.

teach.name: Snapper
cues: Short distance from mouth to eye
look: Emperor: longer mouth-to-eye distance, deeper tail notch
Bream: shorter, rounder body, often a horizontal line

juv.note: Macolor juveniles: black and white pattern, very long pelvic fins. Lutjanus juveniles keep the snapper shape.

teach.name: Emperor
cues: Longer distance from mouth to eye
look: Snapper: short mouth-to-eye distance, shallow tail notch
Bream: shorter, rounder body, often a horizontal line

juv.note: Not very different from adults but not specific at all: early juveniles share a few patterns of stripes and bands, told apart by close examination.

teach.name: Bream
cues: Often a horizontal line along the body
look: Snapper: longer body, shallow tail notch
Emperor: longer body, deeper tail notch

juv.note: Scolopsis bilineata juveniles (black upper half with two yellow stripes) resemble the fangblenny Meiacanthus grammistes, another family. Other Scolopsis: no juvenile source found.

teach.name: Groupers
cues: Ambush predators that suck prey in
High fishing vulnerability: 3rd most exported fish in the Philippines

juv.note: Plectropomus laevis juveniles resemble the Blacksaddle Toby Canthigaster valentini, a pufferfish. Cephalopholis juveniles differ in colour but keep the body plan.

teach.name: Sweetlips
cues: Also called grunts: make sounds by rubbing their tooth plates
phase: Juveniles swim erratically to mimic toxic flatworms
Juvenile, sub-adult and adult look different

juv.trait: head-down, wriggling (undulating) swimming with exaggerated fin movements; bold creamy blotches
juv.note: A resemblance to flatworms or nudibranchs has been suggested, not established.

teach.name: Anthias
phase: Males and females differ in colour

juv.note: No source for the IMR species; for a related one, females and juveniles share one colour description.

teach.name: Boxfish
cues: Bony carapace: square, triangular or rounded
Swims with the dorsal, anal and pectoral fins; tail for bursts of speed
Releases a toxin when in danger

juv.note: Same box shape at all sizes; Ostracion cubicus juveniles are bright yellow with black spots.

teach.name: Goatfish
cues: Two barbels to search the sand for food
Feeds on invertebrates in the sand

juv.note: Barbels at all sizes.

teach.name: Triggerfish
cues: 3 dorsal spines that lock when threatened

teach.name: Pufferfish
cues: Sharp teeth crush invertebrates (crown-of-thorns, urchins, crabs)

juv.note: Arothron stellatus juveniles: orange with dark stripes breaking into spots, unlike the adult but clearly a puffer. Other Arothron and Canthigaster: no juvenile source found.
Thin source: Aluterus scriptus juveniles drift head-down with floating vegetation, offshore.

teach.name: Lionfish
cues: Long, feather-like dorsal and pectoral fins
Native to the Indo-Pacific, invasive in the Caribbean

juv.note: Same feathery fin plan; juveniles mostly translucent.

teach.name: Soldierfish
cues: Reddish body, big eyes; feeds at night
look: Cardinalfish: two widely spaced dorsal fins, small body

teach.name: Cardinalfish
cues: Reddish body, big eyes; feeds at night
First and second dorsal fins widely spaced
Rests still in reef holes or branching corals
look: Soldierfish: tall second dorsal fin, blunt snout

teach.name: Squirrelfish
cues: Reddish body, big eyes; feeds at night
look: Soldierfish: tall second dorsal fin, blunt snout
Cardinalfish: two widely spaced dorsal fins, small body

teach.name: Lizardfish
look: Sandperch: sits slouched, rounded mouth with thick lips

teach.name: Sandperch
look: Lizardfish: sits arched, triangular mouth with teeth

teach.name: Scorpionfishes
teach.why: scorpionfishes and Rhinopias (lionfishes are the IMR Lionfish entry)

teach.name: Garden eels
teach.why: spotted and spaghetti garden eels on the sand slopes

teach.name: Whale shark

wink.wrong: Bold choice. It's a whale shark, the biggest fish in the sea.

teach.note: A wink, not ID training: unmistakable and fun to meet (whale shark trips from Dauin).

teach.name: Thresher sharks

choices: Moorish idol (banner on the wrong end)
wink.right: Correct. That tail was a strong hint.
wink.wrong: Brave. It's a pelagic thresher: the tail is half the shark.

teach.note: A wink, not ID training: unmistakable and fun to meet (pelagic thresher, Malapascua).

species.name: Chaetodon baronessa
species.check: common name as in the PDF; probably Eastern triangular butterflyfish

species.name: Lutjanus russellii
species.check: common name as in the PDF; probably Russell’s snapper
